paras: The South Baltimore Fourth of July brawl was a street fight between white and Black residents of South Baltimore, Maryland, on July 4, 1881, in which a white man, William Hecker, and a Black man, Isaac Curtis, were shot. Both men were reported fatally or mortally wounded, and a Black man, Thomas H. Ross, was arrested on the charge of shooting Hecker. Papers outside Baltimore carried the case as one of a series of holiday shootings in the city.

The fight took place on West Street near Peach and Plum alleys, which the Baltimore German daily Der Deutsche Correspondent described as a place where many "liederliche" (dissolute) whites and Blacks lived together.

According to the Correspondent, around noon a crowd of colored people stood at the corner of West Street and Plum Alley when someone made a rash remark, and words quickly turned to blows among participants who had been drinking. Colored women and several white people joined the fray. Among the whites was Hecker, a 42-year-old German cooper, who the paper said was searching for his son out of fear the boy was in the crowd and might be hurt.

As Officer Knight led an arrested brawler past him, a colored man standing at a cellar door near Peach Alley raised a pistol and fired, and the bullet struck Hecker in the chest. Knight pointed out the shooter to Officer Bayne, who arrested him; at the station house he gave his name as Thomas H. Ross, 24, son of a West Street carpenter and undertaker. Hecker was carried to his home at 1 Peach Alley, where a physician found the bullet had passed through his right lung, and in a statement taken because of the danger to his life he said he did not know who had shot him.

Later that afternoon Curtis, about 29, was walking along Hanover Street when, the Correspondent reported, several Black men accused him of having taken part in the West Street fight. He denied it, one of them threw a brick at him, and at the same moment he was shot in the abdomen by an unknown hand. Curtis walked to the southern station house and was taken by ambulance to University Hospital, where doctors had little hope he would survive.

Fighting at West Street continued until about 12 or 14 participants had been arrested, several of them with bloody heads and stab wounds. Ross was held on the charge of shooting Hecker, while no arrest was reported for the shooting of Curtis. No report of either man's death, of a hearing for Ross or of a trial appears in the coverage found.

The fullest account came from Der Deutsche Correspondent, which headlined it "Blutige Schlägerei in Süd Baltimore" and singled out its German victim with the subhead "Ein deutscher Böttcher daS Opfer." The paper ran the Curtis shooting as a separate item under the question "Wer ist Her Thäter?" (Who is the culprit?).

A Baltimore dispatch of July 4, printed the next day by the Washington National Republican and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, called it a "difficulty" between whites and blacks and described Hecker as a white man "who was near." A shorter wire, run by the Memphis Daily Appeal under "Baltimore's Fourth of July—The City Keeps up its Reputation" and by the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, said only that both men were "fatally wounded" in a fight between whites and blacks. The Washington Evening Star listed the two shootings among eight or ten in Baltimore that day, hedging the charge against Ross with "as is alleged." Three days later the Middletown Transcript in Delaware condensed the story to two sentences in its news column.

The wire dispatch said Curtis was "engaged in the affray" when he was shot, while the Correspondent placed his shooting on Hanover Street after the fight and reported that he denied having taken part. The Correspondent stated that Ross had shot Hecker, but it also reported Hecker's own statement that he did not know who fired, and the Evening Star treated the charge as an allegation.

reader.title: South Baltimore Fourth of July brawl (1881)
bases: The papers describe a street brawl between whites and Black residents in which a white man was shot, allegedly by a Black man, and a Black man was later shot by an unknown hand after being confronted by other Black men (A1, A2, A3, A5); none describes a white attack on Black people.

The local German-language report (A1, A2), the Evening Star roundup (A3) and the Baltimore wire dispatches (A5, A6, A7) agree that Hecker and Curtis were both shot in South Baltimore on July 4 and that Ross was arrested for shooting Hecker.

accounts.label: Local German-language report
accounts.gist: A rash remark among a crowd of colored people at West Street and Plum Alley set off a general brawl; a colored man at a cellar door fired a pistol and hit Hecker, and Ross was arrested. Separately, Curtis was accused by several Black men of having been in the fight, denied it, was hit with a brick and shot by an unknown hand.

accounts.label: Baltimore wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A 'difficulty' between whites and blacks in South Baltimore left Hecker, a white man 'who was near', shot; Ross was arrested on the charge; Curtis, 'engaged in the affray', was shot and thought mortally wounded.

accounts.label: Short wire brief
accounts.gist: During a fight between whites and blacks in South Baltimore, Hecker and Curtis were both 'fatally wounded'.

accounts.label: Evening Star roundup
accounts.gist: Among eight or ten people shot in Baltimore, Hecker was shot 'as is alleged' by Ross, and Curtis was shot in the abdomen 'by some one unknown'.

framing.detail: The Baltimore German paper headlined 'Blutige Schlägerei in Süd Baltimore. Ein deutscher Böttcher daS Opfer', stressed the German victim, and described the neighborhood as one where 'liederliche' (dissolute) whites and Blacks lived together and the brawlers as drunk.
Out-of-town papers ran the case inside roundups of Baltimore's holiday shootings, such as 'Baltimore's Fourth of July—The City Keeps up its Reputation' and 'Fire-Arms in Baltimore'.
The Evening Star's 'Wholesale Shooting in Baltimore Yesterday' hedged Ross's guilt with 'as is alleged'.
